title: Slave and emperor
hook: Epictetus enslaved, Marcus on the throne: one school, very different lives

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musonius Rufus and philosophy for women too. Your line was philosophy for everyone. Who did you share an idea with? Day two hundred ninety-six.

Two men. One was born into slavery, in a town in what's now Turkey. He was owned, sent where he was told, and tradition says he walked with a limp. The other was born generations later into a wealthy Roman family, was marked out young for the throne, and became emperor of Rome. It's hard to imagine two lives further apart. And yet the second man learned how to live from the first one's words. Today: slave and emperor.
screen: `ONE BORN INTO SLAVERY.` → `ONE PICKED FOR THE THRONE.` → `SLAVE AND EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: The first man is Epictetus. Even his name carries his story: in Greek it means acquired, the kind of word you'd use for property. His owner, Epaphroditus, served at the court of Nero, and at some point the young man heard the lectures of Musonius Rufus, the teacher we met yesterday. Later he was freed. He taught in Rome until the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers, then opened a school in Nicopolis in Greece. He didn't write his teachings down himself. A student named Arrian wrote down his talks, and that's the Discourses and the Handbook this path has been quoting. The second man is Marcus Aurelius. At the start of his Meditations he thanks the people who formed him, and one of them is his tutor Rusticus, for introducing him to the discourses of Epictetus and lending him his own copy. So the emperor learned freedom from the notes of a former slave. And they teach the same thing. What's up to us is our own judgment and choice, and nothing else. Epictetus has an image for it in his Handbook: you're an actor in a play, and the author gives out the parts. Maybe a poor man, maybe a ruler, maybe someone who's lame. Your job is to play the part well; choosing it isn't yours. Coming from a man who was handed slavery, that's not a slogan. And coming from a man handed an empire, it's a warning not to confuse the costume with the person. One school. Two very different parts. The same work.
screen: `EPICTETUS: HIS NAME MEANS ACQUIRED.` · `ARRIAN WROTE DOWN HIS TALKS.` · `MARCUS BORROWS THE BOOK.` · `PLAY THE PART YOU'RE GIVEN WELL.` · then, large: `THE SAME SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Think about the part you were handed. Not chosen: handed. The family, the body, the place and time you were born, the money or lack of it. Just notice it, without judging whether it's fair. Then ask quietly: within this part, what's mine to play well today? Rest with that question. The bell holds the time.
Slave and emperor. Epictetus, born enslaved, and Marcus Aurelius, who ruled Rome: one school, very different lives, the same teaching. Today's word.
Your line: the same school. Today, notice someone whose part is very different from yours, richer or poorer, and remember you're both learning the same work. Day two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Stoicism often study Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius side by side, and reflect on playing well the role life has handed them.

match.prompt: slave and emperor — tap the pairs.
pairs: plays the part well, didn't choose it

myth: the Discourses come from his student Arrian's notes.
he thanks Rusticus for lending him Epictetus's discourses (Meditations 1.7).
a word used for property, fitting for someone born enslaved.

fork.setup: Epictetus says life is like a play. you've been handed a part you'd never pick. what's your job?
fork.reveal: in the Handbook the author gives out the parts; our work is to play ours well, since choosing it isn't ours.

original.note: Greek: acquired, gained; the name of the enslaved philosopher.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoicism was a hobby for rich Romans.
what it means: one teaching held by a former slave and an emperor alike.
what a scholar hears: Meditations 1.7 thanks Rusticus for Epictetus's hypomnēmata; Arrian's notes became the Discourses.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.9.29 (Epictetus and Musonius); Arrian's preface to the Discourses

notes: Epictetus's birth around 50 CE at Hierapolis in Phrygia: approximate and traditional.
Epaphroditus served Nero (as secretary/freedman); confirm framing.
Epictetus attending Musonius while still enslaved: generally accepted from Discourses 1.9.29; confirm.
Meditations 1.7: Rusticus 'communicated to me his own copy' of Epictetus's discourses; paraphrased.
Enchiridion 17 paraphrased (author gives out parts: poor man, cripple, ruler, private person).
Marcus born 121 CE, about seventy years after Epictetus: approximate.

Editor review 2026-10-01: cut uncited dates and counts from the hook (born 'around the year fifty', 'seventy years later'), the superlatives ('one of the richest families', 'the most powerful person in the known world'), 'sold' and 'for most of his life' (now 'tradition says he walked with a limp'); no longer asserts he studied with Musonius while still enslaved; 'never wrote a book' softened to what Arrian's preface supports; cut the stock 'here's what's striking'.
